concepts.label: Biosphere
concepts.what: Thin zone (~20 km) where lithosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere overlap and sustain life. Term coined by Eduard Suess (1875). Life is a geological force — it rerouted rivers, transformed the atmosphere, and locked dead organisms into fossil fuels.

concepts.label: Ecosystem
concepts.what: Functional unit where living organisms (biotic) interact with their physical surroundings (abiotic: soil, water, temperature, light, nutrients) as a working system. Term coined by Arthur Tansley (1935). Energy enters from the Sun; nutrients cycle within the system.

concepts.label: Food Chain and Food Web
concepts.what: Producers fix solar energy → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers (carnivores) → tertiary consumers → decomposers return nutrients. Real ecosystems are food webs (multiple pathways), not linear chains; webs are resilient to single-species loss, chains are not.

concepts.label: Photosynthesis
concepts.what: Process by which green plants, phytoplankton, and other producers capture solar energy and fix it into organic matter. The single entry point for energy into most ecosystems; primary productivity sets the ceiling for every trophic level above.

concepts.label: Ten Per Cent Rule (Ecological Energy Transfer)
concepts.what: Approximately 10% of energy at any trophic level passes to the next; 90% is lost as heat, metabolism, or unavailable matter. Consequence: producers are abundant, apex predators are always rare. An ecological pyramid of energy is always upright. (Lindeman, 1942.)

concepts.label: Ecological Pyramid of Energy
concepts.what: Diagrammatic representation of trophic levels showing energy, biomass, or numbers. The energy pyramid is always upright (10% rule). Explains why Bengal tigers, snow leopards, and Asiatic lions exist in small restricted populations — apex predators can only be rare.

concepts.label: Nutrient Cycling
concepts.what: Nutrients circulate between organisms and the abiotic environment in biogeochemical cycles. Unlike energy (which flows in and is lost as heat), matter is conserved and reused. Carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles are the primary ones.

concepts.label: Carbon Cycle
concepts.what: Plants absorb atmospheric CO₂ via photosynthesis and fix it into organic matter; respiration, decomposition, and combustion release it back. Fossil fuels are carbon locked in the lithosphere over hundreds of millions of years; burning them adds it back faster than the natural cycle can absorb.

concepts.label: Nitrogen Cycle
concepts.what: Atmospheric N₂ fixed into biologically usable forms by soil bacteria (Rhizobium in legume root nodules), lightning, and the industrial Haber-Bosch process; returned to atmosphere by denitrification. Human disruption via fertiliser runoff drives eutrophication in lakes and coastal waters.

concepts.label: Phosphorus Cycle
concepts.what: Slowest of the major cycles; no atmospheric reservoir — limited by the rate at which rocks weather. World's accessible phosphate deposits concentrated in a few countries (Morocco, China, Russia). An agricultural bottleneck increasingly visible as demand for fertiliser grows.

concepts.label: Biodiversity — Three Levels
concepts.what: Variety of life at three simultaneously important levels: genetic diversity (gene variation within a species), species diversity (count of distinct species), and ecosystem diversity (variety of habitat types). Losing an ecosystem type can eliminate hundreds of species simultaneously.

concepts.label: Genetic Diversity
concepts.what: Variation of genes within a species; the raw material of adaptation and plant breeding. India's 50,000-200,000 traditional rice landraces represent a genetic reservoir built over millennia. Standardising to high-yield varieties narrows the genetic capital breeders will need for the next disease or climate shift.

concepts.label: Species Diversity
concepts.what: Count of distinct species in a given area. Species richness follows a gradient from equator to poles (more species per unit area in the tropics). India holds ~91,000 described animal species and ~46,000 plant species — ~8% of all known species on 2.4% of the planet's land.

concepts.label: Ecosystem Diversity
concepts.what: Variety of habitat types — wetlands, mangroves, alpine meadows, coral reefs, deciduous forests — each with its own assemblage and set of services. Lose a habitat type and you lose hundreds of species simultaneously, including many not yet identified.

concepts.label: Latitudinal Gradient in Species Richness
concepts.what: More species per unit area in tropical regions, fewer toward higher latitudes. Explanatory hypotheses: greater solar energy input, climatic stability over geological time, more time for speciation, species-area relationship, intermediate disturbance hypothesis. India's biodiversity reflects tropical placement combined with Gondwana-Asia biogeographic inheritance.

concepts.label: Megadiverse Countries
concepts.what: 17 countries defined by UNEP's World Conservation Monitoring Centre as holding ~70% of the world's biodiversity. India on the list alongside Brazil, Indonesia, Colombia, Ecuador, China, Mexico, Australia, and others. A broad frame — biodiversity hotspot concept is the sharper tool.

concepts.label: Biodiversity Hotspot (Norman Myers)
concepts.what: Defined by Norman Myers (1988, refined 2000): ≥1,500 endemic vascular plant species AND >70% original primary vegetation lost. 36 hotspots globally, covering ~2.4% of Earth's land but harbouring ~50% of plant endemics and ~60% of terrestrial vertebrate endemics.

concepts.label: Endemic Species
concepts.what: Species found nowhere else — existence tied to a single landscape. India: Asiatic lion (Gir only), one-horned rhinoceros (Brahmaputra plains only), Nilgiri tahr (Western Ghats only), Indian wild ass (Rann of Kutch only). If the landscape goes, the species goes.

concepts.label: Western Ghats – Sri Lanka Hotspot
concepts.what: One of the world's eight 'hottest hotspots.' Sahyadri system + highland Sri Lanka. ~5,000 plant species; 192 endemic freshwater fish in the Western Ghats alone; lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, shola grassland-forest mosaics above 1,500 m found nowhere else.

concepts.label: Eastern Himalaya Hotspot
concepts.what: Bhutan, northeastern India, parts of Nepal. Abrupt altitudinal rise from Brahmaputra valley floors to Himalayan peaks creates one of the world's highest concentrations of plant species. Red panda, clouded leopard, takin, hundreds of orchid species.

concepts.label: Indo-Burma Hotspot
concepts.what: Extends across northeastern India south of the Brahmaputra through Myanmar, Thailand, Indochina. India's contribution: hoolock gibbon (India's only ape), Irrawaddy dolphin in northeastern river systems, several endemic turtle species.

concepts.label: Sundaland Hotspot (Nicobar Islands)
concepts.what: Reaches India only at the Nicobar Islands. Nicobar megapode, leatherback turtle nesting beaches, species assemblages more closely related to Southeast Asia than to the Indian mainland — biological signature of the Sundaland plate's distinct geological origin.

concepts.label: Rodgers and Panwar — 10 Biogeographic Zones of India
concepts.what: 1988 classification: Trans-Himalaya, Himalaya, Indian Desert, Semi-Arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula, Gangetic Plain, North-East India, Coasts, Islands. Framework designed to serve as the geographic skeleton for the protected area network. India is not one biological territory; it is ten.

concepts.label: Five Drivers of Biodiversity Loss (IPBES Evil Quintet)
concepts.what: IPBES 2019 Global Assessment: (1) habitat loss and fragmentation (largest — deforestation, wetland drainage, urban growth); (2) overexploitation (hunting, poaching, overfishing); (3) pollution (nitrogen/phosphorus runoff degrades aquatic habitats); (4) invasive alien species; (5) climate change.

concepts.label: Invasive Alien Species
concepts.what: Organisms transported across natural barriers by humans. India: Lantana camara (dominates forest understorey, reduces prey habitat); water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes, chokes Loktak, Chilika); Prosopis juliflora (replaced native vegetation across Thar and semi-arid zones).

concepts.label: Eutrophication
concepts.what: Nutrient (nitrogen and phosphorus) runoff from agricultural fertilisers triggers explosive algal growth in water bodies; decomposition of algae depletes dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones hostile to aquatic life. A direct consequence of the disrupted nitrogen cycle from Haber-Bosch and fertiliser overuse.

concepts.label: IUCN Red List
concepts.what: Global inventory of extinction risk maintained by IUCN (founded 1948, Gland, Switzerland). Categories from Not Evaluated through Extinct. India: Bengal tiger (Endangered), Indian elephant (Endangered), snow leopard (Vulnerable), great Indian bustard (Critically Endangered), gharial (Critically Endangered).

concepts.label: Endangered Species — India's Flagship Cases
concepts.what: Asiatic lion (Gir, Gujarat): 20 individuals in 1900, recovered to 600+ but single-location vulnerability. One-horned rhinoceros: Kaziranga and Manas only. Great Indian bustard: Critically Endangered. Gharial: ~700 today from ~10,000 in 1940s. Vultures: >95% crash in 1990s from veterinary diclofenac.

concepts.label: Constitutional Anchors — Articles 48A and 51A(g)
concepts.what: Article 48A (Directive Principle, 42nd Amendment 1976): state must protect and improve environment, safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty, same amendment): every citizen must protect the natural environment. Neither directly enforceable in court but used as interpretive tools in environmental litigation. Jurisdiction: Concurrent List (Article 246).

concepts.label: Wildlife Protection Act 1972
concepts.what: Foundational statute passed same year as Stockholm UN Conference. Schedule system for protected species (Schedule I = highest protection); framework for national parks and wildlife sanctuaries; state authority to notify protected areas. Indira Gandhi's environmentalism landmark.

concepts.label: Forest Conservation Act 1980
concepts.what: Ended state governments diverting forest land for non-forest use without central approval. After 1980, any diversion requires central government permission. Key check on ad-hoc forest loss driven by development.

concepts.label: Environment Protection Act 1986
concepts.what: Passed in aftermath of Bhopal gas tragedy (1984). Gave the Centre sweeping rule-making powers over environmental standards. Umbrella law under which hundreds of environmental regulations have been issued.

concepts.label: Biological Diversity Act 2002
concepts.what: Implemented India's CBD obligations. Created National Biodiversity Authority (centre), State Biodiversity Boards (states), and Biodiversity Management Committees (local). Introduced access-and-benefit-sharing framework requiring foreign entities to obtain approval and share benefits with local communities.

concepts.label: Forest Rights Act 2006
concepts.what: Acknowledged Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers had been dispossessed of customary rights by colonial forest enclosure. Granted individual and community forest rights — restitution of a historical injustice. Creates structural tension with WPA 1972's inviolate core zones; unresolved, a live feature of Indian conservation law.

concepts.label: CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016)
concepts.what: Mechanism to collect and deploy funds when forest land is diverted: developer funds compensatory afforestation elsewhere. Accountability structure designed to unlock money historically accumulated unspent in state treasuries.

concepts.label: National Parks — India's Network
concepts.what: 106 National Parks; strictest protection — no grazing, forestry, cultivation, or habitation; boundaries fixed by legislation. Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand, 1936, first). Kaziranga (Assam, World Heritage, largest one-horned rhinoceros population). Sundarbans (West Bengal, largest mangrove on Earth). Gir (Gujarat, sole Asiatic lion refuge). Periyar (Kerala, Western Ghats elephants).

concepts.label: Wildlife Sanctuaries and Conservation Reserves
concepts.what: Over 566 wildlife sanctuaries — allow more human activity than national parks, more flexible boundaries. Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves (2003 amendment) provide lighter-touch protection for buffer landscapes and community-managed areas.

concepts.label: Biosphere Reserves
concepts.what: 18 in India, 12 in UNESCO's World Network. Concentric-zone model: core → buffer → transition. Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986, India's first, largest). UNESCO-listed: Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar, Nokrek, Manas, Sundarbans.

concepts.label: In-situ Conservation
concepts.what: Conservation within the natural habitat — protected areas, biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries. Protects species AND the ecosystem they depend on. More effective than ex-situ for maintaining ecological interactions and genetic diversity of wild populations.

concepts.label: Ex-situ Conservation
concepts.what: Conservation outside natural habitat — seed banks, botanical gardens, zoological parks, gene banks, tissue culture. Safety net for species when in-situ protection fails; does not preserve ecological relationships. India: National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (New Delhi) holds one of the world's largest seed banks.

concepts.label: Project Tiger (1973)
concepts.what: Launched 1973; now 54+ Tiger Reserves with strictly protected core and managed buffer zones. Tiger count: ~1,800 in 1973 → 3,682 in 2022. India holds >75% of world's wild tigers. Side effect: tigers expanding into human-dominated landscapes, sharpening human-wildlife conflict in corridor districts.

concepts.label: Project Elephant (1992)
concepts.what: 33+ Elephant Reserves, focused on maintaining corridors between fragmented forest patches. Asian elephant requires unbroken habitat connectivity over hundreds of kilometres that no single reserve can provide; the corridor is the conservation unit.

concepts.label: Ramsar Wetland Sites — India
concepts.what: India has 80+ designated Ramsar sites. Key ones: Chilika Lake (Odisha, largest coastal lagoon in Asia), Loktak Lake (Manipur), Wular Lake (Kashmir), Keoladeo (Rajasthan), Sambhar Salt Lake (Rajasthan). India joined Ramsar Convention 1982.

concepts.label: Project Snow Leopard (2009)
concepts.what: Focuses on the Trans-Himalayan zone (Ladakh, Spiti, Lahaul, upper Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal). Snow leopard is Vulnerable (IUCN). Conservation challenge: vast high-altitude range across multiple countries; pastoralist-predator conflict over livestock.

concepts.label: Vulture Collapse and Diclofenac Ban
concepts.what: Three Indian vulture species (white-backed, long-billed, slender-billed) crashed >95% in the 1990s. Cause: veterinary drug diclofenac — vultures eating treated-livestock carcasses suffered fatal kidney failure. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. Vulture-Safe Zones established. Recovery slow (4-5 years to breeding age) but collapse arrested.

concepts.label: Olive Ridley Sea Turtle — Arribada at Gahirmatha
concepts.what: Olive Ridley turtles mass-nest (arribada) at Gahirmatha beach (Odisha) in one of the world's largest such aggregations. Sea Turtle Conservation programmes protect nesting beaches from light pollution, fishing gear, and human disturbance.

concepts.label: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
concepts.what: Opened at Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit (1992). Three pillars: conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. Access-and-benefit-sharing framework addressed North-South asymmetry: biodiversity in the South, biotechnology industry in the North.

concepts.label: Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000)
concepts.what: Additional agreement to the CBD dealing with living modified organisms (GMOs) and their international trade. India ratified in 2003.

concepts.label: Nagoya Protocol (2010)
concepts.what: Strengthened CBD's access-and-benefit-sharing provisions: genetic resources must be accessed with prior informed consent; benefits must be shared fairly with the country of origin. In force 2014. India ratified in 2014.

concepts.label: CITES
concepts.what: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (1973). Regulates trade via three appendices. Appendix I: bans commercial trade in most threatened species (tigers, elephants, rhinoceros). Appendix II: regulates and monitors. Appendix III: species protected in at least one country.

concepts.label: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (1971)
concepts.what: Signed in Ramsar, Iran (1971). Predates the CBD; focuses on wetland conservation and wise use. India joined 1982. Membership obligates countries to designate Ramsar sites and maintain their ecological character.

concepts.label: IPBES
concepts.what: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (established 2012). Biodiversity equivalent of the IPCC. 2019 Global Assessment (the 'evil quintet' report) is its landmark document. Not a UN organ directly; intergovernmental body with UN facilitation.

concepts.label: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022)
concepts.what: Adopted at CBD COP 15 (2022). Succeeded the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (set COP 10 in 2010; expired 2020 largely unmet). Key goal: '30×30' — 30% of land and oceans under effective conservation by 2030.

concepts.label: Convention on Migratory Species (CMS, Bonn 1979)
concepts.what: Addresses species crossing national boundaries during migration. India is a signatory. Relevant species: bar-headed goose, Amur falcon, flamingos, humpback whale. Conservation requires international coordination across range states.

concepts.label: FRA 2006 vs WPA 1972 — Structural Tension
concepts.what: FRA 2006 grants community forest rights to tribal communities; WPA 1972 requires inviolate core zones in tiger reserves and national parks. The two statutes are structurally in conflict; neither fully implemented; the tension is a live feature of Indian conservation law producing ongoing litigation and policy gridlock.

concepts.label: Western Ghats Eco-Sensitive Zone Debate
concepts.what: Gadgil Committee (2011): ~64% of Western Ghats ecologically sensitive, restricting mining and construction across Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra. Kasturirangan Committee (2013): reduced to ~37%, prioritising development. Neither report implemented in full; political economy has stalled both. The tension is the actual shape of the problem, not a policy design failure.
